name: Manchester
history: Manchester, New Hampshire was originally settled in 1722 and incorporated as a city in 1846, having been renamed from "Derryfield" in 1810 by merchant Samuel Blodget, who envisioned "the Manchester of America" modeled after the industrial city in England. During the nineteenth century, Manchester became home to the Amoskeag Manufacturing Company, then the largest cotton textile plant in the world, which drove massive industrial growth and immigration to the region. The city's economy shifted significantly after World War II as textile manufacturing declined, though it has since diversified and undergone substantial downtown redevelopment.

name: Londonderry
history: The area now known as Londonderry was originally called Nutfield due to its dense woods containing nut trees, with settlers arriving around April 1719 and petitioning for incorporation that September. The town was officially chartered on June 21, 1722, and named after Londonderry in Ulster, Ireland, reflecting the Irish and New England heritage of its founding population. A notable historical achievement occurred in 1719 when the first North American potato was cultivated in what is now Derry, then part of Londonderry, while the town's growth accelerated dramatically after World War II with the construction of Interstate 93.

name: Milford
history: Milford separated from the neighboring town of Amherst in 1794 and, like most towns bearing this name, derives its identity from a mill constructed on a ford of the Souhegan River. The town became renowned for its granite quarries during the nineteenth century, which supplied stone for notable structures including pillars of the U.S. Treasury Building in Washington, D.C. Milford also served as a stop on the Underground Railroad and was home to Harriet E. Wilson, whose 1859 novel Our Nig is recognized as the first published by an African-American woman in the country.

name: Hanover
history: Hanover was chartered on July 4, 1761, by Governor Benning Wentworth, with its first European settlers arriving in 1765-1766 primarily from Connecticut. The town's name likely derives from either a parish in Connecticut or from the reigning British-Hanoverian king George III, referencing the German House of Hanover. In the 1780s, the southwestern area known as Dresden briefly joined the independent Vermont Republic before returning to New Hampshire, a historical remnant still reflected in the interstate Dresden School District that serves both Hanover and Norwich, Vermont.

name: Weare
history: Weare was incorporated in 1764 by Governor Benning Wentworth and named after Meshech Weare, the town's first clerk who later became New Hampshire's first governor. The town experienced a catastrophic flood in 1938 when the New England Hurricane caused the Deering Reservoir dam to breach, destroying mills and devastating sections of the community. In response, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers constructed Everett Dam as part of a flood control project completed in 1963, which resulted in the permanent abandonment of the village of East Weare.

name: Gilford
history: Originally settled in 1778 as part of Gilmanton and known as Gunstock Parish, the town was incorporated in 1812 when Captain Lemuel B. Mason proposed naming it Guilford after the Revolutionary War battle where he had fought in North Carolina, though the name was later contracted by clerical error to Gilford. The town became notable as the destination of the first snow train from Boston in the 1930s and featured New Hampshire's first motorized ski lift, a gasoline-powered rope tow constructed in 1934 at what is now Gunstock Mountain Resort.

name: Plymouth
history: Plymouth was incorporated in 1763 after being granted to settlers from Hollis, many of whom were French and Indian War veterans originally from Plymouth, Massachusetts, from which the town derived its name. The area was originally home to an Abenaki village before being destroyed by British forces in 1712 during Queen Anne's War. Notable historical events include author Nathaniel Hawthorne's death there in 1864 and the founding of the Plymouth Normal School in 1871, which eventually became Plymouth State University.

name: Henniker
history: Henniker was incorporated in 1768 by Governor John Wentworth and named after Sir John Henniker, a London merchant engaged in the leather and fur trade with shipping interests in Boston and Portsmouth. The town developed as an agricultural and industrial center, with water-powered mills along the Contoocook River supporting operations including a woolen factory until their closure in 1959. In the nineteenth century, Henniker experienced a notably high rate of congenital deafness and developed its own sign language, which scholars believe may have influenced the development of American Sign Language.

name: Loudon
history: Loudon was incorporated on January 23, 1773, by Governor John Wentworth, with territory taken from the neighboring town of Canterbury. The town was named to honor John Campbell, 4th Earl of Loudoun, a Scottish military leader who commanded British forces in North America during the French and Indian War. Lord Loudoun notably helped establish Rogers' Rangers, an independent colonial militia company attached to the British Army during the conflict.

name: Barnstead
history: Barnstead was granted in 1727 and incorporated as a town in 1767, with its name deriving from settlers who emigrated from Barnstable, Massachusetts, and Hempstead, New York. The town's rolling terrain proved ideal for agricultural development, supporting approximately 2,500 sheep by 1830 and becoming a significant lumber manufacturing center by the mid-nineteenth century, with mills, factories, and tanneries powered by the Suncook River.

name: Northwood
history: Northwood was incorporated on February 6, 1773, when colonial governor John Wentworth separated a large tract of land called "North Woods" from the adjacent town of Nottingham. Around 1800, the construction of the Portsmouth to Concord Turnpike stimulated economic growth, leading to the establishment of numerous taverns and eventually twelve sawmills, five of which later transformed into shoe factories during the nineteenth century. The town has since evolved into a recreational destination, becoming known for its nine lakes and antique shops.

name: New London
history: New London was incorporated in 1779 by sixteen families who petitioned the General Court, officially taking its name from London, England, though possibly also acknowledging the Londonderry-based proprietors who had recruited the original settlers. The township proprietors systematically subdivided and sold their properties at substantial profit, with nearly all initial settlers coming from Massachusetts towns like Amesbury and Attleboro. In 1947, Colby-Sawyer College became the permanent site of the Gordon Research Conferences, establishing the town as a center for scientific gatherings.

name: Tilton
history: Originally the southern part of Sanbornton known as "Sanbornton Bridge," the area was incorporated as the town of Tilton in 1869 and named in honor of Nathaniel Tilton, an early settler who established an iron foundry and the region's first hotel. The town's development was significantly shaped by Charles E. Tilton, the great-grandson of Nathaniel and a wealthy textile mill owner, who donated numerous statues and landmarks to the community, including his mansion which now houses the Lucian Hunt Library and a notable Roman arch replica built of Concord granite as a memorial to his ancestors.

name: Campton
history: Campton was granted by Governor Benning Wentworth in 1761 and incorporated in 1767, with initial settlement beginning around 1765. The town derives its name from a camp that the first proprietors established to survey the two towns of Campton and Rumney. By the mid-nineteenth century, Campton had developed a diverse local economy including sawmills, gristmills, tanneries, and carriage manufacturing, and the town remains notable for its three covered bridges, including the Blair Bridge, which ranks among the longest entirely within New Hampshire.

name: Tamworth
history: Tamworth was granted in 1766 by colonial Governor Benning Wentworth and named in honor of British Vice-Admiral Washington Shirley, Viscount Tamworth, a close friend of the governor. The town became a destination for prominent thinkers and artists during the early twentieth century, including philosophers William and Henry James and poet E.E. Cummings, who sought refuge in the White Mountains region. The Barnstormers Theatre, established in 1931 by Francis Cleveland, son of President Grover Cleveland, remains among the oldest continuously running professional summer theaters in the country.

name: Madison
history: Madison was incorporated in 1852 as a town in Carroll County, New Hampshire, named in honor of President James Madison on the centennial of his birth. The area had previously been designated for land grants to soldiers who served in the French and Indian War, covering parts of what are now Eaton and Albany. Today, Madison is notable for being home to the Madison Boulder, the largest known glacial erratic in New England and among the largest in the world.

name: Canterbury
history: Canterbury was first granted by Lieutenant Governor John Wentworth in 1727 and incorporated in 1741, being named after William Wake, the Archbishop of Canterbury. Originally established as a militia timber fort and trading post by Captain Jeremiah Clough where the Pennacook people came to trade, the town would later become home to the Canterbury Shaker Village, established in 1792, which at its peak housed over 300 residents across 4,000 acres and is now preserved as a National Historic Landmark.

name: Colebrook
history: Colebrook was initially granted in 1762 as "Dryden" but regranted and renamed in 1770 by Governor John Wentworth after Sir George Colebrooke, chairman of the East India Company, with formal incorporation occurring on June 11, 1796. The remote settlement experienced early hardship when its first inhabitants were driven out by the Revolutionary War, with meaningful development only resuming afterward. The town subsequently became a significant center for potato starch production in the nineteenth century, at its peak generating roughly one third of the potato starch in the state, before transitioning to dairy farming after 1880.

name: Alstead
history: Alstead was incorporated in 1763 and named for Johann Heinrich Alsted, a scholar whose encyclopedia was widely read at Harvard College. Originally chartered by Massachusetts Governor Jonathan Belcher in 1735 as part of a defensive line of forts, the town became known as "Paper Mill Village" after Ephraim and Elisha Kingsbury established one of New Hampshire's first paper mills there in 1793. The town briefly joined Vermont in 1781 following the Revolutionary War but returned to New Hampshire authority at George Washington's urging.

name: Lyndeborough
history: Originally granted by the Massachusetts General Court to veterans from Salem, Massachusetts, the area was initially known as "Salem-Canada" before being renamed Lyndeborough following a re-grant to proprietors that included Benjamin Lynde, who would become Chief Justice of Massachusetts. John Cram and his family established the first settlement in 1736 with a sawmill, and the town was incorporated in 1764. The town has maintained significant historical institutions, including the Lafayette Artillery Company, which relocated there in 1833, and numerous structures now listed on the National Register of Historic Places, such as the 1846 town hall and Citizens' Hall from 1889.

name: Dublin
history: Dublin was incorporated in 1771 by Governor John Wentworth and named after the Irish birthplace of early settler Henry Strongman, who had relocated from Peterborough. The town developed as a farming community with rocky soil, though its population declined significantly after the mill town of Harrisville separated from it in 1870. Notably, in 1912, 'Abdu'l-Baha, the leader of the Baha'i Faith, spent 23 days in Dublin and gave several high-profile addresses on topics including racial equality and spiritual education.

name: Wilmot
history: Wilmot was incorporated in 1807, formed from territories that included parts of New London, the Kearsarge gore, and a small section of New Chester. The town derives its name from Dr. James Wilmot, an English clergyman who had spoken out against England's treatment of the American colonies. A notable historical connection exists through Winslow State Park, which honors Captain John Winslow, commander of the USS Kearsarge, the Civil War naval vessel that sank the CSS Alabama in 1864.

name: Richmond
history: Richmond was first chartered in 1735 as "Sylvester-Canada" to honor Captain Joseph Sylvester of Massachusetts, who died in 1690 during a military campaign in Canada, and was incorporated in 1752 under its present name by Governor Benning Wentworth, who named it after Charles Lennox, the 3rd Duke of Richmond, a proponent of colonial independence. The town was settled beginning around 1757 by emigrants from Rhode Island and Massachusetts, and historically developed a notable pail-making industry that became central to its economy.

name: Jackson
history: Jackson was incorporated in 1829 and named after President Andrew Jackson, who had just been inaugurated. The town's origins trace back to 1778 when Benjamin Copp and his family first settled the area, which had previously been called "New Madbury" in honor of a coastal New Hampshire town. By the mid-nineteenth century, Jackson became a notable resort destination, attracting White Mountain School artists beginning in 1847 and subsequently developing into a popular tourist hub served by railroad lines that brought up to 40 trains daily by the 1920s.

name: Wentworth
history: Wentworth, New Hampshire was granted and incorporated in 1766 by Governor Benning Wentworth, who named the town after himself, and was settled primarily by residents arriving from Massachusetts towns like Salisbury. The town developed into a lumber-producing center powered by the Baker River's water resources, operating nine sawmills until a catastrophic 1856 flood destroyed most of these mills and significantly widened the river channel.

name: Goshen
history: Goshen, New Hampshire was incorporated in 1791 after being first settled in 1768 as part of the town of Saville, which later became Sunapee. The town's name may derive from Goshen, Connecticut, where many early residents had family connections. In 1954, Goshen established a cooperative elementary and middle school with neighboring Lempster that operated for over six decades until the arrangement dissolved in 2016.

name: Sullivan
history: Sullivan, a town in Cheshire County, New Hampshire, was incorporated on September 27, 1787, and named after General John Sullivan. The community was established through portions of four neighboring towns: Gilsum, Keene, Nelson, and Stoddard, with farming emerging as its primary economic activity. In 1867, Sullivan became the first town in New Hampshire to dedicate a monument to its soldiers lost in the Civil War, a monument that stands across from the Sullivan Congregational Church.

name: Stark
history: Stark, New Hampshire was granted in 1774 and originally named "Percy" after Hugh Percy, 1st Duke of Northumberland, before being incorporated in 1795 and renamed in 1832 to honor General John Stark, the Revolutionary War figure whose words inspired the state motto "Live Free or Die." During World War II, the town hosted Camp Stark, which held approximately 250 German prisoners of war and served as the only World War II POW camp located in New Hampshire. Many of these prisoners performed labor in local forests to supply wood for paper mills in nearby Berlin before the camp closed in 1946.

name: Randolph
history: Randolph was originally granted as "Durand" in 1772 and later incorporated as a town in 1824, taking its name from John Randolph, a Virginia congressman and senator descended from Pocahontas. The town developed as a vacation destination in the nineteenth century, with hotels like the Mt. Crescent House drawing visitors via train and horse-drawn carriage before automobiles became prevalent. In 1910, the Randolph Mountain Club was established to restore trails destroyed by logging, and it continues operating camps and shelters throughout the surrounding White Mountain National Forest.

name: Ellsworth
history: Ellsworth, New Hampshire was originally chartered as "Trecothick" after a Boston-born merchant and Lord Mayor of London, but was renamed in 1802 to honor Chief Justice Oliver Ellsworth. The town's first census in 1800 recorded 47 residents, establishing it as a small rural community in Grafton County. Today, the entire municipality lies within the White Mountain National Forest and is home to part of the Hubbard Brook Experimental Forest, making it an important site for environmental research.

name: Nashua
history: Originally part of a Massachusetts tract called Dunstable, the area was incorporated as Nashua in 1836 when the New Hampshire portion was renamed after the Nashua River, whose name derives from the Nashaway people and means "beautiful stream with a pebbly bottom" in the Penacook language. The city developed as a major textile manufacturing hub during the Industrial Revolution, with the Nashua Manufacturing Company operating four mills and employing approximately 1,000 people by the mid-1800s. After the textile industry declined following World War I, the arrival of defense contractor Sanders Associates (now BAE Systems) in a former mill helped revitalize the city's economy in the mid-twentieth century.

name: Hudson
history: Hudson's origins trace to the Dunstable Land Grant, with the area eventually becoming Nottingham West in 1739 before adopting its present name in 1830 to avoid confusion with the older Nottingham. The town's name apparently derives from an early misconception that the Merrimack River connected to the Hudson River, or from exploration by Henry Hudson, though both explanations proved unfounded. A significant aspect of Hudson's development came through the Alfred and Virginia Hills family, whose substantial land donations to the town, including Alvirne High School and the Hills Memorial Library, shaped the community's educational and cultural institutions for generations.

name: Exeter
history: Exeter was founded on April 3, 1638, when clergyman John Wheelwright, exiled from Massachusetts, purchased land and established the town, naming it after Exeter in Devon, England. Originally inhabited by Pennacook Abenaki people who called the area "M'Squamskook," meaning "Falls at the Place of the Salmon," the settlement became one of four original townships in the province. The town served as New Hampshire's capital for fourteen years beginning in 1774, after the Provincial Congress relocated there to escape the royal governor's restrictions on meeting in Portsmouth.

name: Somersworth
history: Somersworth was organized as a parish in 1729 and incorporated as a town in 1754 by colonial governor Benning Wentworth, with its name deriving from "Summersworth," meaning "summer town" because ministers preached there during that season. The city became a major mill town in the 19th century after the Wendell brothers established the Great Falls Manufacturing Company in 1822, which operated textile mills that specialized in producing drillings, shirtings, and sheetings along the Salmon Falls River. Somersworth was incorporated as a city in 1893 and later experienced significant labor unrest, including participation in the 1922 New England Textile Strike before the regional textile industry entered decline in the mid-20th century.

name: Hampstead
history: Hampstead was incorporated in 1749 by colonial governor Benning Wentworth, who named it after Hampstead, England, the residence of William Pitt, a close friend. Originally settled in 1640 and initially known as "Timberlane Parish" due to its dense forests, the town was formed following the 1739 boundary decision between Massachusetts and New Hampshire. The town became home to the first honey factory in the United States, established in 1816.

name: Stratham
history: Stratham was settled in 1631 and formally incorporated in 1716 as the sixth town in the colony, named after Wriothesley Russell, Baron Howland of Streatham, a friend of Royal Governor Samuel Shute. The area was originally called Winnicutt by the Pennacook people and known as "Squamscott Patent" or "Point of Rocks" due to its geographic location. Notably, Stratham was comprehensively mapped by Phinehas Merrill in 1793, making it unusual among New England settlements of comparable size and allowing historians to identify which extant buildings predate the map.

name: Meredith
history: Originally chartered as Palmer's Town in 1748 by the Masonian Proprietors in honor of surveyor Samuel Palmer, the settlement was renamed New Salem before receiving its current name in 1768 from Governor John Wentworth, who chose to honor Sir William Meredith, 3rd Baronet, a member of Parliament who opposed taxation on the colonies. The town's development accelerated in the early 1800s when John Bond Swasey constructed an innovative canal system that redirected water from Lake Waukewan, creating powerful waterfalls that powered numerous mills and eventually the Meredith Electric Light Company by 1895. Connected by railroad in 1849 and later served by steamboat routes from nearby Alton Bay, Meredith transformed into a thriving summer resort destination.

name: New Boston
history: New Boston was first granted as a township in 1736 by colonial governor Jonathan Belcher and formally incorporated in 1763 under Governor Benning Wentworth, who formally recognized the long-used name of "New Boston" after settlers from Boston families had called it by that name since around 1751. The town developed into an industrial center, boasting 25 sawmills, six grain mills, two clothing mills and other manufacturing operations by 1820, though much of the lower village was destroyed during the Great Village Fire of 1887. In the twentieth century, New Boston became home to the Gravity Research Foundation and later the New Boston Space Force Station, a military satellite tracking facility established during the Cold War.

name: Rye
history: Rye was incorporated in 1785, though it was originally established as a parish in 1726 and called "Sandy Beach" before being renamed "Rye" after the town of Rye in Sussex, England, ancestral home of the prominent local Jenness family. The area has deeper roots as the site of the first European settlement in New Hampshire, Pannaway Plantation, established in 1623 at Odiorne's Point by English fishermen led by David Thompson, though this settlement was later abandoned. The town experienced tragedy during King William's War when a band of Wabanaki Indians attacked Sandy Beach in a raid in September 1691 in what became known as the Brackett Lane Massacre.

name: Northfield
history: Northfield was incorporated as an independent town on March 30, 1780, after residents of the northern area of Canterbury petitioned the state legislature for separation, citing the difficulty of traveling to the town center for civic business. The town derived its name from the "north fields" designation that had been used for this region of Canterbury since the 1740s. Following the arrival of the Boston, Concord and Montreal Railroad in 1848, Northfield developed into a mill town, leveraging the water power of the Winnipesaukee River to establish textile and paper manufacturing that sustained its economy throughout the nineteenth century.

name: Haverhill
history: Settled by citizens from Haverhill, Massachusetts, the town was initially known as "Lower Cohos," a name derived from the Abenaki people who had an agricultural presence in the area, before being incorporated in 1763 by colonial Governor Benning Wentworth. The town became the county seat of Grafton County in 1773 and served as the terminus of the Province Road, which connected northern and western settlements to the seacoast. Haverhill is home to the Haverhill-Bath Covered Bridge, constructed in 1829 and recognized as the oldest documented covered bridge in the country still standing.

name: Ossipee
history: Originally called "Wigwam Village" and later "New Garden," Ossipee was incorporated as a town on February 22, 1785, and named for the Ossipee Indians, one of twelve Algonquian tribes. The settlement was the site of an Indian stockade fort built to defend against Mohawk attacks; after its destruction in 1725, Captain John Lovewell rebuilt it into one of the largest in New England. In the 19th century, Ossipee developed into a resort community, particularly after the Portsmouth, Great Falls & Conway Railroad reached the area in 1871, bringing commerce and tourism to the town.

name: Hinsdale
history: Hinsdale was chartered in 1753 and named for Colonel Ebenezer Hinsdale, a Harvard graduate and military officer who established Fort Hinsdale, including a trading post and gristmill, in 1742. Located beside the Connecticut River in southwestern New Hampshire, the town became an important center for industrial manufacturing, particularly papermaking, and was home to George A. Long, who built an early steam-powered vehicle in his machine shop during the 1870s. The town's earliest decades were marked by conflict with Native Americans, involving raids, assaults, and captivities.

name: Sunapee
history: Sunapee was incorporated in 1781 after undergoing several name changes, including "Saville," "Corey's Town," and "Wendell," before the legislature adopted the name "Sunapee" in 1850. The town's name derives from Algonquian words meaning "goose" and "water," as indigenous peoples called the area the "Lake of the Wild Goose" due to the lake's distinctive shape. Before becoming a tourist destination centered around Lake Sunapee, the town served as an industrial hub, with one factory producing 110 clothespins per minute.

name: Thornton
history: Thornton was granted on July 6, 1763, and incorporated on November 20, 1781, receiving its name in honor of Doctor Matthew Thornton, a signer of the Declaration of Independence. Located in Grafton County, the town developed as part of New Hampshire's early settlement expansion in the late eighteenth century and grew to encompass 50.7 square miles across the Pemigewasset River watershed.

name: Whitefield
history: Whitefield was chartered on July 4, 1774, as the last town to be granted under the English provincial government, and was incorporated under its current name on December 1, 1804. The town's name possibly derives from George Whitefield, a renowned English evangelist connected to Dartmouth College's patron, though some attribute it to the snowy white fields visible through surrounding mountain passages. Following the arrival of railroads in the nineteenth century, the town became a popular tourist destination for visitors seeking refuge from urban heat and pollution, leading to the construction of several grand hotels including the Mountain View House in 1866, which later became one of New Hampshire's most luxurious resorts.

name: New Hampton
history: The town was granted in 1765 by Governor Benning Wentworth and originally named "Moultonborough Addition" after Colonel Jonathan Moulton, who later changed it to "New Hampton" in 1777 when the town was incorporated, taking inspiration from his birthplace of Hampton. In 1821, the New Hampton School, a Free Will Baptist institution, was established in the town, and by 1920 it became home to the state's oldest fish hatchery.

name: Holderness
history: In 1751, Thomas Shepard petitioned colonial Governor Benning Wentworth on behalf of 64 grantees for land on the Pemigewasset River, and the town was named after Robert Darcy, 4th Earl of Holderness, though settlement was delayed by the French and Indian War until after 1759. The land was regranted as "New Holderness" in 1761 and first settled in 1763, with proprietor Samuel Livermore attempting to establish a grand estate modeled on English countryside estates. By the mid-nineteenth century, the town had developed into a resort destination, attracting tourists who traveled by steamboat along Squam Lake, and it remains popular for recreation, notably serving as the filming location for the 1981 movie On Golden Pond.

name: Middleton
history: Middleton was granted by the Masonian Proprietors in 1749 and named after Sir Charles Middleton, 1st Baron Barham, who oversaw convoy services between Barbados and the colonies. The town was incorporated on March 4, 1778, after initial settlement by pioneers from nearby communities shortly before the Revolutionary War. Following the war, a significant population of Quaker families, led by town auditor Nicholas Austin, relocated to Quebec in search of a more peaceful environment.

name: Effingham
history: Effingham was initially settled by members of the Leavitt family from Hampton, New Hampshire and was known as "Leavitt's Town" before being renamed by Governor Benning Wentworth in 1749 in honor of the Howard family, Earls of Effingham who were related to the Wentworths by marriage; the town was incorporated in 1778. By the mid-19th century, Effingham Falls had developed into a significant mill town featuring textile and wood processing facilities, and the town became the home of New Hampshire's first normal school, established in 1830 to train teachers under the direction of future U.S. Senator James W. Bradbury.

name: Unity
history: The area that became Unity was originally chartered in 1753 as "Buckingham" before being incorporated under its current name in 1764, following the resolution of land grant disputes between Massachusetts and New Hampshire colonial authorities. The town developed into a significant industrial center, and by 1810 it had grown to over 1,000 residents with multiple mills and a thriving sheep farming industry. In 2008, Unity gained national attention when presidential candidates Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton held their first joint public appearance there, a choice reportedly made because of the town's meaningful name and because the candidates had each received exactly 107 votes from Unity voters during the Democratic primary.

name: Grafton
history: Grafton was originally granted in 1761 and re-granted in 1769, taking its name from Augustus FitzRoy, 3rd Duke of Grafton, before being formally incorporated in 1778. Historically, the town's economy was based on subsistence farming, small-scale industry, and mining, with mica mines and granite quarries, notably Ruggles Mine, once characterizing the local landscape. The town later became known in the early 2000s as the focus of a libertarian settlement initiative that ultimately dissolved in 2016 amid various complications.

name: Washington
history: Washington was incorporated on December 13, 1776, by the newly established American revolutionary government and named after George Washington, making it one of the first named in his honor. Originally settled in 1768, the town developed into a manufacturing center that utilized water power to produce lumber, textiles, and other goods, while also supporting sheep farms that generated wool and mutton for regional commerce. The establishment of the first Seventh-day Adventist church in Washington in 1862 marked a significant religious development in the community's history.

name: Hill
history: Originally incorporated as "New Chester" in 1753, the town was renamed "Hill" in 1837 to honor Isaac Hill, who served as governor of New Hampshire from 1836 to 1839. A significant event in the town's development occurred in 1941, when the village of Hill was relocated to accommodate the construction of the Franklin Falls Dam.

name: Warren
history: Warren was granted in 1763 by Governor Benning Wentworth and incorporated in 1770, taking its name from Admiral Sir Peter Warren of the Royal Navy. The town's most distinctive landmark is a Redstone ballistic missile displayed on the village green, donated in 1971 to honor Senator Norris Cotton, a Warren native. From 1909 to 1970, the village of Glencliff served as the mailing address for the New Hampshire State Sanatorium, a tuberculosis treatment facility located on Mount Moosilauke's slopes.

name: Piermont
history: Piermont was incorporated by Governor Benning Wentworth in 1764 and settled four years later, deriving its name from Italy's Piedmont region. The town boasts a notable connection to Western expansion through Aaron Lane, a Piermont native who became the first permanent settler in the area that would develop into Victorville, California. Colonel William Tarleton, a delegate to the Constitutional Convention of 1791, left his mark on the community by giving his name to Lake Tarleton, which remains a prominent local landmark.

name: Langdon
history: Langdon was first settled in 1773 by Seth Walker and officially incorporated on January 11, 1787, receiving its name after Governor John Langdon. The town is notable as the home of the Prentiss Bridge, constructed in 1874 across Great Brook, which holds the distinction of being New Hampshire's shortest covered bridge at just 34 feet 6 inches in length.

name: Landaff
history: Landaff was originally granted as "Whitcherville" in 1764 but was re-granted to Dartmouth College in 1770 after the initial settlers forfeited their claim, and the town was formally incorporated on November 11, 1774. The town's name derives from its official charter designation "Llandaff," honoring the Bishop of Llandaff who served as chaplain to King George III. After the Revolutionary War, the original grantees successfully challenged the forfeiture as illegal, forcing Dartmouth College to relinquish its claims and abandon the infrastructure investments it had made in establishing settlements.

name: Dummer
history: Dummer was granted in 1773 by Governor John Wentworth to Portsmouth investors and named after Massachusetts Governor William Dummer, who successfully defended English provinces during Dummer's War. The town remained largely unsettled until 1812 when William Leighton arrived with his family, and it was officially incorporated in 1848. The local economy developed around timber resources and water power from the Upper Ammonoosuc River, with sawmills and log drives eventually supplying papermills downstream in Berlin.

name: Hart's Location
history: Hart's Location, incorporated in 1795, was named after Colonel John Hart of Portsmouth, New Hampshire, following a 1772 land grant to Thomas Chadbourne. The town gained historical prominence through the tragic 1826 Willey family disaster, when a landslide killed the family despite their house remaining standing, an event that inspired Nathaniel Hawthorne's short story "The Ambitious Guest." Since 1948, Hart's Location has become nationally recognized for frequently being one of the first places to report results in New Hampshire's presidential primary and general elections.

name: Concord
history: The area was first settled by Europeans in 1659 as Penacook, and the town was incorporated as Rumford on February 9, 1734, before receiving its current name in 1765 when Governor Benning Wentworth renamed it to reflect "the new harmony" following a boundary dispute with the neighboring town of Bow. In 1808, Concord was designated the official seat of state government, and the State House, completed in 1819, remains the oldest capitol building in which a state legislature continues to meet in its original chambers. The city became a significant economic center in the nineteenth century through furniture manufacturing, granite quarrying, and the famous Abbot and Downing Company's Concord coaches, which played an important role in western expansion.

name: Bedford
history: The area was initially established in 1733 by the Province of Massachusetts Bay as "Narragansett, No. 5" as a land grant for soldiers who had fought against the Narragansett people in Rhode Island. The settlement was officially incorporated as "Bedford" in 1750 and named after John Russell, 4th Duke of Bedford, a close friend of Governor Benning Wentworth who served as Secretary of State for the Southern Department. The town experienced rapid growth during the second half of the twentieth century, expanding from approximately 2,176 residents in 1950 to over 18,000 by 2000, driven largely by its proximity to Manchester.

name: Windham
history: Originally settled by Scots-Irish immigrants beginning in 1719 as part of the "Nutfield" region, Windham was formally incorporated as an independent town in 1742 when Governor Benning Wentworth granted a petition from local settlers. The town's name likely derives either from Windham, Ireland, reflecting the settlers' heritage, or alternatively from Sir Charles Wyndham, 2nd Earl of Egremont, a British politician and friend of Governor Wentworth. Among its notable historical landmarks is Searles Castle, completed in 1915 by interior decorator Edward Francis Searles and designed by architect Henry Vaughan to resemble Stanton Harcourt Manor in England.

name: Amherst
history: Amherst was incorporated on January 18, 1760, when New Hampshire Governor Benning Wentworth chartered the settlement and renamed it after General Jeffery Amherst, who served as Commander-in-Chief, North America during the French and Indian War. The town became the county seat of Hillsborough County in 1770 due to its strategic location along the region's primary east-west transportation corridor. Following World War II, Amherst experienced significant population growth as it became integrated into the Greater Boston metropolitan area, transforming from a relatively stagnant settlement into a thriving suburban community.

name: Franklin
history: Franklin was settled by English colonists in 1764 as "Pemigewasset Village" at the confluence of two rivers before being incorporated as a town in 1828 and later as a city in 1895. The settlement adopted the name "Franklin" in 1820 in honor of statesman and founding father Benjamin Franklin. The town developed into a mill community powered by waterfalls on the Winnipesaukee River, and in 1943 the Army Corps of Engineers constructed the Franklin Falls Dam nearby for flood control purposes.

name: Belmont
history: Belmont was originally chartered in 1727 as "Upper Gilmanton," a parish of Gilmanton, and developed into a mill town powered by the Tioga River before being incorporated as an independent municipality on June 28, 1859. The town adopted its current name in 1869 in honor of financier August Belmont, though he never acknowledged the gesture. The Belmont Mill, built in 1833 to manufacture textiles and later hosiery until its closure in 1955, underwent a celebrated adaptive reuse project from 1996 to 1998 that earned regional and national preservation awards.

name: Sandown
history: Originally part of Kingston, Sandown was established as an independent town in 1756 under colonial governor Benning Wentworth and named after "the picturesque Sandown on the Isle of Wight." The Reverend Josiah Cotton, the town's first minister, constructed the Sandown Meeting House in 1774, which remains a notable example of early New England church architecture featuring an 11-foot-high pulpit and marble columns.

name: Littleton
history: Originally called "Chiswick" and settled in 1769, the town was granted as "Apthorp" in 1770 to honor George Apthorp, a wealthy Boston merchant, before being renamed Littleton in 1784 when incorporated to honor Colonel Moses Little, a landowner and Surveyor of the King's Woods. The town's industrial heritage includes the Littleton Grist Mill, which opened in 1798 along the Ammonoosuc River, and the Kilburn Brothers factory, which produced and sold stereoscopic photographs and viewers between 1867 and 1909.

name: Jaffrey
history: Jaffrey, New Hampshire was first granted in 1736 to soldiers returning from Canada and subsequently incorporated in 1773 by Governor John Wentworth, receiving its name for George Jaffrey, member of a wealthy Portsmouth family. The town's development was powered by water mills along the Contoocook River and later attracted notable visitors and residents, including Ralph Waldo Emerson and Henry David Thoreau, who were drawn to the scenic beauty of Mount Monadnock.

name: Deerfield
history: Deerfield was incorporated in 1766 after residents initially petitioned for separation from Nottingham in 1756, a request that was denied until local hunters presented colonial governor Benning Wentworth with a deer, inspiring the town's name. Originally a thriving agricultural community, Deerfield was disappointed by the railroads' bypass in the nineteenth century, prompting citizens to establish the Deerfield Fair in 1876, now known as "New England's Oldest Family Fair." The town also housed Deerfield Academy, a high school founded around 1798 that burned in 1842.

name: North Hampton
history: North Hampton was first settled in 1639 as part of Hampton, originally known as "North Hill" or "North Parish," before being incorporated as an independent township in 1742 by colonial governor Benning Wentworth following New Hampshire's separation from Massachusetts. The town's name derives from its geographic position north of the original Hampton settlement. During the nineteenth century, the seaside area of Little Boar's Head developed into a fashionable resort destination, featuring elegant Victorian and Edwardian architecture that remains notable today.

name: Strafford
history: Strafford was incorporated as a town in 1820, having been "set off due to the lengthy travel required to attend town meetings" from the neighboring town of Barrington. The town takes its name from Strafford County, which was established in 1773 and named to honor Thomas Wentworth, 1st Earl of Strafford. A notable institution, the Austin-Cate Academy, was established in 1904 through the philanthropic efforts of shoe manufacturer George Cate, whose substantial bequest transformed the local educational landscape until the property was eventually acquired by the state for a National Guard training center.

name: Gilmanton
history: Gilmanton was incorporated in 1727 and named after the Gilman family, who originally settled in Exeter and received land grants in the newly established town, along with related families including the Dudleys, Leavitts, Folsoms, and Coffins. Once the second-largest town in New Hampshire after Portsmouth, Gilmanton later became widely recognized in the 1950s when author Grace Metalious, a resident of the town, published the popular novel Peyton Place, which was rumored to be based on the community.

name: Bristol
history: Bristol was incorporated on June 24, 1819, after being separated from the towns of Bridgewater and New Chester, with settlement beginning in 1770 under Colonel Peter Sleeper and Benjamin Emmons. The town derives its name from "extensive deposits of fine sand or clay similar to the Bristol Sand used in Bristol, England, to make fine china and pottery," with local sand instead being manufactured into superior quality brick. During the nineteenth century, Bristol developed into a manufacturing center powered by the Newfound River, producing goods including paper, leather, woolens, and other textiles, while also becoming a popular tourist destination along Newfound Lake beginning in the mid-1800s.

name: Gorham
history: Gorham was incorporated as a town in 1836, though it had been chartered in 1770 as part of Shelburne and first settled around 1802. The town was named at the suggestion of resident Lot Davis, who was from Gorham, Maine, and a relative of the Gorham family that incorporated that Maine town in 1764. The arrival of the St. Lawrence and Atlantic Railroad in 1851 transformed Gorham into a major railroad hub with locomotive yards and repair facilities, which in turn brought tourism and led to the construction of several hotels that served travelers heading to Mount Washington and the White Mountains.

name: Bethlehem
history: Originally granted as "Lloyd's Hills" in 1774 to honor James Lloyd of Boston, the town was incorporated under its current name on December 27, 1799, after residents rejected the Loyalist connection and selected the new designation on Christmas Day. Following the arrival of railroad service in 1867, Bethlehem transformed into a prominent Gilded Age resort destination, eventually hosting over 30 hotels and attracting wealthy visitors and notable figures including multiple U.S. Presidents. The town later became known for its significant Jewish community, which grew beginning around 1916 as families sought relief from hay fever in the town's low-pollen environment.

name: Fitzwilliam
history: Fitzwilliam was originally granted as "Monadnock No. 4" in 1752 and incorporated in 1773, when Governor John Wentworth named it after his cousin William Fitzwilliam, 4th Earl Fitzwilliam. The town was established as part of a line of eight communities settled by Scottish colonists and became notable as the home of early grantees including Matthew Thornton, a signer of the Declaration of Independence, and James Reed, who later led forces at the Battle of Bunker Hill. The community developed significant industries including one of New Hampshire's oldest granite quarries, woodworking, and yarn-making before the railroad arrived in 1848.

name: Sutton
history: Sutton was granted in 1749 by the Masonian Proprietors to settlers from Massachusetts and New Hampshire, initially named "Perrystown" after proprietor Obadiah Perry, though settlement was delayed by the French and Indian War until 1767. The town received its current name from Sutton, Massachusetts, source of settlers who arrived after the town was regranted in 1784. In 1981, Sutton became home to the world's first paintball facility, operated by Bob Gurnsey, one of paintballing's inventors, which remained open until 1985.

name: Alexandria
history: Granted in 1753 by the Masonian Proprietors and incorporated on November 23, 1782, Alexandria was named for Alexandria, Virginia, the site of a 1755 governors' conference during the French and Indian War. The town was first settled in 1769 by John Moore Corliss and his brother Jonathan. Alexandria holds historical significance as the birthplace of Luther C. Ladd, who became "the first enlisted soldier to lose his life in the Civil War" when he was shot during the 1861 Baltimore Riot.

name: Freedom
history: Freedom was incorporated in 1831 as a town that had previously been called "North Effingham," a part of the larger town of Effingham. The community received its name to commemorate its separation from Effingham following cultural and religious conflicts between Maine settlers and established residents from New Hampshire's seacoast region. The town has since become known as a location for several educational and recreational institutions, including being the setting for Oliver Butterworth's 1956 children's fantasy novel The Enormous Egg.

name: Bennington
history: Bennington was incorporated in 1842 from portions of several neighboring towns in an area previously known as "Society Land." The town was named to commemorate the 1777 Battle of Bennington, an American Revolutionary War engagement fought in nearby Vermont, which itself was named after New Hampshire governor Benning Wentworth. Situated at the Great Falls of the Contoocook River, Bennington developed into an industrial center with mills and factories, including a gristmill established in 1782 and a paper mill constructed in 1835 that would eventually become the Monadnock Paper Mills.

name: Temple
history: Temple was incorporated in 1768 by colonial Governor John Wentworth, who named the town after John Temple, his lieutenant governor. The settlement began in 1758 when Maj. Ephraim Heald and his family arrived as among the first settlers, with Peter Heald becoming recognized as the town's founder. A notable early industry was the Temple Glassworks, established in 1780 by Robert Hewes of Boston, whose products became "rare and prized collectibles" despite the company's eventual closure.

name: Bridgewater
history: Bridgewater was incorporated on February 12, 1788, and was named after Bridgewater, Massachusetts, by settlers who originated from that town. Originally part of a larger settlement called New Chester, the land was first settled in 1776 by Thomas Crawford before being separated into five distinct towns. The community gained railroad connectivity in 1874 when the Montreal railroad established a station there, and later became known as a summer retreat for acclaimed author John Cheever.

name: New Castle
history: New Castle was incorporated on May 30, 1693, and took its name from Fort William and Mary, an earthwork defense originally built on Fort Point that evolved into the namesake fort. The town gained prominence as the site of one of the American Revolution's first military actions when colonists raided Fort William and Mary on December 14, 1774, seizing gunpowder and weapons that would later be used at the Battle of Bunker Hill. Originally settled in 1623 on Great Island at the mouth of the Piscataqua River, New Castle became the easternmost and smallest town in New Hampshire, and remains the only municipality in the state located entirely on islands.

name: Carroll
history: Land was granted to Sir Thomas Wentworth and others in 1772, with the township initially named "Bretton Woods" after Wentworth's English estate. The town was formally incorporated on June 22, 1832, as Carroll in honor of Charles Carroll, a signer of the Declaration of Independence. The area became renowned for tourism in the late nineteenth century, culminating in the construction of the Mount Washington Hotel in 1902, which later hosted the 1944 International Monetary Conference that established the International Monetary Fund and World Bank.

name: Albany
history: Albany was originally chartered in 1766 by colonial Governor Benning Wentworth as "Burton," named after General Jonathan Burton of Wilton, New Hampshire. The community was incorporated and renamed "Albany" in 1833, coinciding with the chartering of the New York Central Railroad from New York City to Albany, New York. The town is also home to the World Fellowship Center, "an intergenerational camp and conference retreat center founded in 1941 by and for peace activists."

name: Sugar Hill
history: Sugar Hill was incorporated as a town in 1962, making it the most recently incorporated town in New Hampshire, having been separated from the town of Lisbon following considerable legal disputes. The town derives its name from "the large groves of sugar maples within the town limits." During the Victorian era, Sugar Hill became a fashionable resort destination, attracting wealthy visitors from major eastern cities to its panoramic mountain views, and it notably hosted the nation's first resort-based ski school, established in the early 1900s at Peckett's-on-Sugar Hill Inn.

name: Eaton
history: Eaton was established in 1766 by colonial Governor Benning Wentworth and named after Governor Theophilus Eaton of Connecticut, "a generous contributor to the funds needed to settle Massachusetts in 1630." The town's notable landmarks include the "Little White Church" overlooking Crystal Lake, and the village of Snowville, which takes its name from the Snow family who established a sawmill there in 1825.

name: Errol
history: Errol was granted in 1774 by Governor John Wentworth to Timothy Ruggles and others, with its name derived from Scotland's James Hay, 15th Earl of Erroll. The town was officially incorporated in 1836, after its first settlers arrived in 1806 and the population had grown to 36 by 1820. Historically, the town's economy centered on lumbering due to its vast forests, and by 1859 it supported two sawmills, one gristmill, and one clapboard machine despite having generally poor soil.

name: Derry
history: The area was first settled by Scots-Irish families in 1719 as part of Londonderry, and Derry was incorporated as a separate town in 1827 from the eastern portion of that original settlement. Like its parent town, Derry was named after the city of Derry in Ireland, with the Irish word "Doire" meaning "oak grove." The town claims two notable historical distinctions: it was the site where the first potato planted in the United States was sown in a common field in 1719, and it is the birthplace of astronaut Alan Shepard, the first American in space, earning it the nickname "Spacetown."

name: Keene
history: Keene was initially granted as the township of "Upper Ashuelot" in 1735 to sixty-three settlers, then regranted and renamed in 1753 by Governor Benning Wentworth after Sir Benjamin Keene, a principal of the South Sea Trading Company. The settlement was attacked and burned by Native Americans during King George's War in 1747, though colonists returned to rebuild in 1749. In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, Keene developed as a regional commercial and educational center, eventually becoming the county seat and home to two colleges.

name: Durham
history: Originally settled by English colonists in 1622 and incorporated as a township in 1732, Durham was renamed from its former designation as Oyster River Plantation, though the exact origin of the name "Durham" remains unclear. The town gained national prominence when it became the site of a significant 1694 attack during King William's War, in which French forces and Abenaki warriors killed over 100 inhabitants and destroyed much of the settlement. In the nineteenth century, Durham's trajectory changed dramatically when Benjamin Thompson bequeathed his estate to establish an agricultural college, which eventually became the University of New Hampshire in 1923, transforming the town into an academic center.

name: Raymond
history: Raymond was originally settled as a parish of Chester known as "Freetown," a name arising from the ship timber business, and was incorporated as a town in 1764 under its new name, which according to historical records means "the lustrous, luminous or shining world." In 1906, philanthropist Andrew Carnegie provided a grant toward constructing a library in the town, which opened as the Dudley-Tucker Library in 1908. The town's railroad connection, established in 1850 on the line between Concord and Portsmouth, eventually became part of the Boston and Maine Railroad's Portsmouth Branch before passenger service ceased in 1954.

name: Litchfield
history: Originally part of the town of Dunstable established in the 1600s, the area was first incorporated into Massachusetts on July 4, 1734, and was renamed "Litchfield" in 1749 after George Henry Lee, Earl of Lichfield, when it was incorporated into the Province of New Hampshire. Prior to European colonization, the region was inhabited by the Abenaki people, who left behind over 30 Native American archaeological sites along the Merrimack River. The town experienced significant population growth beginning in the 1970s as it transformed from farmland into a bedroom community for the Greater Boston area.

name: Swanzey
history: Originally granted in 1733 as "Lower Ashuelot," the town was regranted and incorporated in 1753 by Governor Benning Wentworth under the name "Swanzey," most probably because early settlers had connections to Swansea in Wales. Situated on the Ashuelot River, the town developed into an industrial center, with West Swanzey becoming a textile mill town and East Swanzey gaining recognition for wooden bucket production. The area experienced significant conflict during King George's War, forcing its abandonment for three years before its reestablishment.

name: Rindge
history: Rindge was incorporated in 1768 by Governor John Wentworth and named in honor of Captain Daniel Rindge of Portsmouth, New Hampshire, one of the original grant holders. The town's early settlement was interrupted by territorial disputes and King George's War, but permanent habitation resumed in the 1750s, leading to steady growth supported by numerous water-powered mills throughout the 19th century.

name: Auburn
history: Auburn, New Hampshire was originally settled by Native Americans in 1624 as a fishing community called "Massabesic," though British settlers arrived in 1720 and the area was later known by various names including "Chester Woods" and "Long Meadow" before becoming an independent town on June 25, 1845. Like several other American towns bearing the same name, Auburn took its designation from Oliver Goldsmith's 18th-century poem "The Deserted Village," which opens with the line "Sweet Auburn! loveliest village of the plain." The town was historically served by the Concord and Portsmouth Railroad, which later became part of the Boston & Maine Railroad system, though freight service ceased in the early 1980s.

name: Chester
history: Chester was incorporated on May 8, 1722, originally under the name Cheshire before adopting its current designation, likely derived from Chester, the county town of Cheshire in England. The settlement began in 1719 when approximately eighty residents from Portsmouth and Hampton established an association to secure land in the region then known as the "Chesnut Country." Over its early history, Chester underwent significant territorial changes, with Candia being set off as a separate town in 1763 and portions later transferred to Hooksett and Auburn.

name: Epsom
history: Epsom was incorporated in 1727 and takes its name from Epsom in Surrey, England. The town's landscape of small mountains proved suitable for grazing and grain cultivation, supporting two gristmills and two sawmills by 1859. On April 24, 1944, a military aircraft crashed on a local mountain, claiming all ten occupants aboard.

name: Lee
history: Lee was established on January 16, 1766, when Colonial Governor Benning Wentworth granted it a charter, making it among the last of 129 towns to receive a charter during his administration. The settlement was named after British General Charles Lee, who subsequently participated in the American Revolution. During King William's War, Wheelwright Pond within Lee's territory became the site of a significant 1690 battle when colonial forces pursued Indigenous attackers, resulting in heavy casualties on both sides including three officers and fifteen soldiers.

name: Winchester
history: Winchester, New Hampshire was originally established in 1733 as "Arlington" by colonial Governor Jonathan Belcher to protect the Massachusetts Bay Colony border, then incorporated in 1753 under its current name by Governor Benning Wentworth in honor of Charles Paulet, 3rd Duke of Bolton and Marquess of Winchester. The town's early settlers faced repeated attacks by Indigenous peoples, and the community was burned in 1745 before gradually developing into an agricultural center with various small industries, including an early musical instrument manufacturer and textile mills following the arrival of the Ashuelot Railroad in 1850.

name: Wilton
history: Wilton was incorporated in 1762 and is believed to have been named either for the town of Wilton in England or for Sir Joseph Wilton, a renowned English sculptor whose coach design for King George III's coronation later influenced the Concord coach model. Originally chartered as "Salem-Canada" in 1735 and intended as a frontier settlement to protect against Indigenous attacks, the town developed around water-powered textile mills along the Souhegan River before evolving into a rural residential community. In May 1816, Wilton established what may have been the first Sunday school in the United States devoted exclusively to religious instruction, led by two local women and connected to the town's Congregational church.

name: Lancaster
history: Lancaster was granted as "Upper Coos" in 1763 and settled beginning in 1764 by David Page Jr. and Emmons Stockwell, making it the first settlement north of Haverhill. The town was subsequently named after Lancaster, Massachusetts, the hometown of an early inhabitant. Notable early residents included Reverend Joshua Weeks, who helped name the Presidential Range mountains, and grantees Timothy Nash and Benjamin Sawyer, who discovered Crawford Notch in 1771, establishing a crucial shorter route to Portland, Maine.

name: New Durham
history: New Durham, originally granted as "Cochecho Township" in 1749, was first settled by Europeans in 1750 primarily by colonists from the nearby town of Durham, from which it derived its name. The town was officially incorporated as New Durham on December 7, 1762, and its rocky terrain led settlers to focus on grazing and lumber production, with five sawmills and four shingle mills operating by 1859. The town gained religious significance as the birthplace of the Free Will Baptist denomination, founded by local minister Benjamin Randall in 1780.

name: Tuftonboro
history: Tuftonboro was granted as "Tuftonborough" in 1750 by colonial Governor Benning Wentworth and incorporated by the New Hampshire Legislature on December 17, 1795, taking its name from John Tufton Mason, who initially owned the undivided lands of northern New Hampshire as heir to the Masonian Claim. The town was notably the only incorporated place in New Hampshire owned by just one man before Mason sold the property to Portsmouth merchants in 1746, who then distributed it to settlers prior to the American Revolution. By the mid-nineteenth century, Tuftonboro's economy centered on livestock husbandry and light manufacturing, including sawmills, carriage factories, and gristmills.

name: Newbury
history: The town of Newbury was incorporated in 1837 under a name suggested by settlers originally from Newbury, Massachusetts. Prior to its current designation, the settlement had been known by several names reflecting different historical grants and ownership: it was initially called "Dantzic" after the Baltic seaport, then "Hereford" in 1754 to honor a Viscount, and "Fishersfield" in 1772 for John Fisher. The town's development was shaped by its location on Lake Sunapee, which became a significant feature attracting both residents and visitors to the region.

name: Greenville
history: Greenville was incorporated as a town in 1872, having previously been part of Mason Village. Located at the High Falls on the Souhegan River, the town developed as a manufacturing center due to the abundant water power, with the Columbian Manufacturing Company established in 1826 to produce textiles for both Greenville and neighboring New Ipswich. The brick mill buildings from this industrial era still dominate the village landscape today, though most have been repurposed for modern uses such as businesses, storage, and elderly housing.

name: Newfields
history: Settled in 1638 and originally called "Newfield Village," the community remained part of other towns until Dr. John M. Brodhead donated his library and $10,000 to the town in 1880 on the condition it be renamed "Newfields," leading to its incorporation under that name in 1895. A notable early development was the 1775 construction of a bridge across the Squamscott River connecting Newfields to Stratham, which shortened travel to Exeter but ultimately bypassed the town center, preserving its historic character. The community's architectural heritage includes garrison houses built for protection against Indigenous attacks, reflecting its colonial frontier origins.

name: Bradford
history: Bradford was granted in 1765 and incorporated on September 27, 1787, taking its name from settlers who arrived in 1774 from Bradford, Massachusetts. The town developed into an industrial center by the mid-nineteenth century, with the Concord & Claremont Railroad reaching Bradford in 1850 and serving as the line's terminus until its extension to Claremont in 1871-1872. By 1859, the town supported diverse manufacturing operations including woolen mills, sawmills, and a gristmill, leveraging the water power provided by local streams.

name: Rumney
history: Rumney was established as a town when Governor Benning Wentworth granted it in 1761 to settlers from Connecticut, though it was first settled in 1765 and subsequently regranted in 1767. The town takes its name from Robert Marsham, 2nd Baron Romney, whose title was pronounced similarly. The settlement developed a diverse economy based on fertile farmland, and by 1859 included fifteen sawmills, a tannery, and a ladder factory, with railroad service arriving to West Rumney in 1850-1851.

name: Stoddard
history: Stoddard was incorporated in 1774 and named in honor of Colonel Sampson Stoddard, a surveyor who had received the land grant but never lived there. The town was first settled in 1768 by Irish immigrants John and Martha Taggart, and by 1800 its population of 1,148 residents exceeded that of the nearby county seat of Keene. Between 1840 and 1873, Stoddard became a renowned center of glass manufacturing, producing distinctive amber and olive-toned glassware whose unique hues resulted from trace minerals in the local sand, making Stoddard glass highly valued by collectors today.

name: Lempster
history: Lempster was first granted in 1735 as "Number 9" by colonial governor Jonathan Belcher, then regranted in 1753 as "Dupplin" before receiving its final name in 1767, derived from Sir Thomas Fermor, Second Baron Leominster or "Lempster," and was incorporated in 1772. The town developed as a rural settlement in Sullivan County, and in 2008 it became home to New Hampshire's first wind farm, a facility with 12 turbines generating 24 megawatts of power located on Bean Mountain.

name: Harrisville
history: Harrisville was incorporated in 1870 from lands ceded by five neighboring towns and was named after Milan Harris, whose Cheshire Mills operated as a textile manufacturer. Originally known as "Twitchell's Mills" when a sawmill and gristmill were constructed in 1774, the town developed into a prosperous industrial center following the 1878 opening of the Manchester & Keene Railroad. The town is notable for being the only industrial community of the early 19th century to endure in its original form, with its distinctive red brick mills and historic district preserved as a National Historic Landmark.

name: Surry
history: Surry was chartered in 1769 and named after Charles Howard, the 10th Duke of Norfolk and Earl of Surrey. The town's first census in 1790 recorded 448 residents, reflecting early settlement in this Cheshire County community. The area is notable for Surry Dam on the Ashuelot River, which creates Surry Mountain Lake as a recreational resource, and for being the hometown where Amos Pollard, the chief surgeon and defender of the Alamo, grew up.

name: Brookfield
history: Brookfield was settled in 1726 by Scots-Irish immigrants who initially called it "Coleraine" after a town in Northern Ireland, before it was renamed after Brookfield, Massachusetts and finally incorporated on December 12, 1794, following a separation from the town of Middleton. The division had been motivated by geographical obstacles, as the long, high ridge of the Moose Mountains made it difficult for residents on opposite sides to attend town meetings. In 1874, the Wolfeborough Branch Railroad extended service through the town, further connecting it to the wider region.

name: Hebron
history: Hebron was first settled in 1765 and incorporated in 1792 from portions of the extinct township of Cockermouth and the area then known as West Plymouth. Early settlers, predominantly from New England towns, initially pursued farming as their primary occupation, though economic activity diversified after construction of the Mayhew Turnpike in 1803 facilitated connections with southern cities and lumber mills. By the 1920s, the town had developed tourism as a major industry, featuring summer lodges and winter skiing attractions.

name: Benton
history: Benton was chartered on January 31, 1764, by Governor Benning Wentworth and originally named Coventry after the Connecticut hometown of many early settlers. The town was renamed Benton in 1840 at the suggestion of Governor Isaac Hill, honoring U.S. Senator Thomas Hart Benton of Missouri, a prominent advocate for westward expansion. By the mid-nineteenth century, the town's mountainous terrain and abundant forests supported a thriving lumber industry with five sawmills operating by 1859.

name: Clarksville
history: Clarksville was incorporated in 1853 and renamed in 1872 to honor the Clark family, who had purchased the land that was originally part of a "Dartmouth College Grant." In the late nineteenth century, the town's economy relied on starch and maple sugar production before logging companies became the primary employers for many years.

name: Dover
history: Dover was settled in 1623 when brothers William and Edward Hilton established a permanent settlement at Pomeroy Cove, making it the oldest permanent settlement in New Hampshire and seventh in the United States. The city takes its name from Dover, Kent in England, with the word deriving from the Brythonic word for "waters." A significant early tragedy occurred on June 28, 1689, when the settlement suffered a devastating attack by Native Americans seeking revenge for an incident thirteen years earlier in which Major Richard Waldron had tricked hundreds of Native American warriors into a mock battle and subsequently had many captured or killed.

name: Portsmouth
history: Portsmouth was incorporated as a town in 1653 and named after the English port city of Portsmouth in Hampshire, honoring colony founder John Mason who had served as captain there. Originally called Strawbery Banke by European settlers who arrived in 1630, the city became a prosperous seaport engaged in fishing, lumber, and shipbuilding. It later played a significant role in American history, hosting the negotiations that produced the Treaty of Portsmouth ending the Russo-Japanese War.

name: Hooksett
history: Hooksett was incorporated in 1822, having previously been known as "Chester Woods" and "Rowe's Corner" before adopting its present name. The town's name possibly derives from a hook-shaped island in the Merrimack River or from early fishermen who referred to the area as "Hookline Falls." In 1794, the community became connected to regional commerce when the lottery-funded Hooksett Canal was constructed to serve mills along the river.

name: Conway
history: Conway was chartered in 1765 by colonial Governor Benning Wentworth and named after Henry Seymour Conway, who later became Commander in Chief of the British Army. The region had previously been home to the Pequawket, an Algonquian Abenaki tribe, until disease and conflict led to their withdrawal by the early 18th century. By the mid-1800s the town became a destination for landscape artists drawn to the White Mountains, and the arrival of railroads in 1871 transformed it into a major tourism center.

name: Seabrook
history: Seabrook was incorporated on June 3, 1768, as a town in what is now Rockingham County. Located at the southern end of New Hampshire's coastline, the town developed as a coastal settlement and is the first municipality encountered when traveling northbound on Interstate 95 into the state. In the modern era, Seabrook gained prominence as the site of the Seabrook Station Nuclear Power Plant, which began operations in 1990.

name: Pembroke
history: Pembroke was initially granted in 1728 as "Lovewell's Town" before being renamed "Suncook" after the local river, and finally incorporated in 1759 under its current name honoring Henry Herbert, the ninth Earl of Pembroke. The town's early economy centered on water-powered mills producing print cloth and brick manufacturing along the Merrimack River, with the arrival of the Concord and Portsmouth Railroad in 1852 further facilitating development. New Hampshire's geographic center of population is located near Pembroke's town center.

name: Peterborough
history: Peterborough was granted by Massachusetts in 1737 and incorporated on January 17, 1760, by Governor Benning Wentworth, receiving its name after Lieutenant Peter Prescott (1709-1784) of Concord, Massachusetts, a prominent land speculator. The town became a prosperous mill center during the 19th century, with its first cotton factory established in 1810 and multiple textile and manufacturing operations flourishing along its waterways. Notably, Peterborough established the first tax-supported free public library in the United States in 1833.

name: Hillsborough
history: Originally granted in 1735 as "Number Seven," a defensive settlement under Massachusetts, the town was renamed Hillsborough in 1748 after Sir Wills Hill, Earl of Hillsborough, and incorporated in 1772. The town gained national prominence as the birthplace of Franklin Pierce, the 14th President of the United States and the only president from New Hampshire, whose homestead is now a National Historic Landmark. Hillsborough is also home to a cluster of five 19th-century stone arch bridges designated as a National Historic Civil Engineering Landmark.

name: Nottingham
history: Nottingham was incorporated in 1722 by Lieutenant Governor John Wentworth and named after Daniel Finch, 2nd Earl of Nottingham, a close friend of previous colonial governors. The town became historically significant as the site of a 1747 conflict and later produced four Revolutionary War generals. In the modern era, Nottingham established itself as an environmental pioneer, becoming one of the first towns in the nation to make recycling mandatory when its recycling center opened in January 1974.

name: Newton
history: Newton was incorporated by colonial governor Benning Wentworth in 1749 as "Newtown," simply because it was a new town, with the name later contracted to "Newton" by the New Hampshire legislature in 1846. Originally part of various Massachusetts towns and parishes, residents sought incorporation due to the distance from their church. Newton was the sixth town granted from the Masonian land purchase of 1746.

name: Brentwood
history: Brentwood was incorporated on June 26, 1742, when colonial governor Benning Wentworth set it off from the town of Exeter. The town takes its name from Brentwood in Essex, England, originally called "Burnt Wood," where King Henry II granted permission in 1177 for forest land to be cleared and cultivated. Following its separation from Exeter, Brentwood experienced internal disputes over meetinghouse location, and its western portion eventually became the town of Fremont in 1764.

name: Pittsfield
history: Pittsfield was settled in 1768 by families from Hampton, New Hampshire, and incorporated as a town in 1782, having previously served as an unnamed parish of Chichester. The town takes its name from William Pitt, the British Prime Minister and great friend of the colonies prior to the American Revolution. Early development was shaped by founder John Cram, who established grist and sawmills in the late eighteenth century, while the town later became home to Globe Manufacturing, which has produced protective firefighter clothing since 1901.

name: Canaan
history: Canaan was chartered in 1761 by Governor Benning Wentworth and named after Canaan, Connecticut, the hometown of many early settlers who had themselves named their town after the biblical land of Canaan. The town experienced significant development following the arrival of the Northern Railroad in 1847, which spurred industrial growth including water-powered mills. It gained tragic historical prominence following a 1907 train collision that claimed 26 lives, remaining the deadliest railroad accident in New Hampshire history.

name: Bartlett
history: Settled after 1769 and incorporated in 1790, Bartlett was named for Dr. Josiah Bartlett, one of New Hampshire's signers of the Declaration of Independence and an early state governor. The town's development as a railroad community began in 1875 when the Maine Central Railroad's Mountain Division was constructed through the area. In the twentieth century, tourism became central to the local economy, particularly following the opening of Story Land in 1954 and Attitash ski area in the 1960s.

name: Chichester
history: Chichester was granted in 1727 to Nathaniel Gookin and others, receiving its name from Thomas Pelham-Holles, the 1st Duke of Newcastle-upon-Tyne and Earl of Chichester, who served as England's Secretary of State for the Southern Department. The first permanent settlement began in 1758 when Paul Morrill established himself in the area. The Chichester Grange Hall, which now houses town offices, has been recognized as a historic structure and is listed in the State Register of Historic Places.

name: Plainfield
history: Plainfield was incorporated in 1761 by colonial governor Benning Wentworth and named after Plainfield, Connecticut, from which its first settlers originated. The town became associated with the Cornish Art Colony, most notably through artist Maxfield Parrish, who purchased land nearby in 1898 and resided there for decades, even painting the stage backdrop in the Plainfield Town Hall. The village of Meriden, located within the town, became home to Kimball Union Academy, established in 1813.

name: Troy
history: Troy was settled in 1762 and incorporated in 1815 after being set off from Marlborough, with portions also drawn from Fitzwilliam, Swanzey, and Richmond. The town's name reflected the presence of the family of Samuel Wilson, the man famously known as "Uncle Sam," who was connected to Troy, New York. The town's economy was historically anchored by Troy Mills, which began making horse blankets in the mid-19th century and dominated local industry for nearly a century before declaring bankruptcy in 2001.

name: Ashland
history: Ashland was incorporated in 1868 as a separate town, having formerly been part of Holderness, and was named for Ashland, the Kentucky estate of statesman Henry Clay. The town's economy was historically driven by water power from the Squam River falls, which enabled sawmills and gristmills beginning in the 1770s, followed by textile manufacturing that dominated the community into the twentieth century. Ashland has since transitioned from its industrial past into a residential and resort destination, with the last textile mill closing in 2002.

name: Lyme
history: Lyme was established as a town in 1761 when colonial Governor Benning Wentworth granted it along with many other towns along the Connecticut River, though actual settlement did not occur until 1764 when residents primarily from Massachusetts and Connecticut arrived. The town's name derives from Lyme in Connecticut, following the common practice of New England settlers naming new communities after their places of origin. Notable historical features include a Congregational church bell cast by Paul Revere in 1815 and a remarkable row of 27 horse sheds from 1810, said to be the longest line of contiguous horse sheds in New England.

name: Lincoln
history: Lincoln was granted to Connecticut land investors by colonial Governor Benning Wentworth in 1764 and named after Henry Fiennes Pelham-Clinton, the 9th Earl of Lincoln. Settlement began around 1782, and the town developed into a logging center by the mid-nineteenth century, with timber and water power from the Pemigewasset River driving its economy.
